title: Evidence for the Court
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · The Doll Test and Brown v. Board
objective: Students will follow one strand of evidence in *Brown v. Board of Education*, from the separate schools of the Brown cases, through the Clarks’ doll tests and Kenneth Clark’s testimony, to the unanimous decision of May 17, 1954 and its footnote 11. They will weigh what the doll tests could show.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: In 1954 the Supreme Court decided that separate schools are inherently unequal. Part of the evidence came from two psychologists who listened to young children.

items.text: explain what the Brown cases were about, and where they came from
items.question: explain what the Brown cases were about?

items.text: describe what Kenneth and Mamie Phipps Clark’s doll tests set out to study, and what they found
items.question: describe what the doll tests studied, and what they found?

items.text: trace how the doll tests became evidence: in Clarendon County, in court and in footnote 11
items.question: trace how the doll tests reached the Supreme Court?

items.text: evaluate the doll tests as evidence: what they could show, and why they became a symbol of the Brown case
items.question: evaluate the doll tests as evidence?

materials: *Who Do You See?*, *The Doll Test* tab (online), projected
Page 3 of this plan; differentiated handouts
connection: **Online,** *Who Do You See?* tells the Doll Test step by step for the projector, with a question and teacher’s notes at each step, and ends on poster 2: *“The introduction of the first Black Barbie was a monumental step toward inclusivity, offering Black children a doll that reflected their identity and celebrated their cultural heritage.”* **In the exhibition,** stand with the class at poster 2 and the display case.

steps.title: One sentence from the Court
script: Project the Court’s sentence and read it slowly: *“Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”* Ask: *“What does it claim? What would a court need, to be sure of that?”* *“Today we follow one piece of the evidence: it came from two psychologists, and some dolls.”*

screen.text: Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.
screen.cite: Brown v. Board of Education, May 17, 1954

steps.purpose: Start from the Court’s conclusion, and ask what evidence could support it.
students: What would a court need, to be sure of that?

steps.title: Separate schools
script: Read: *“In each of the Brown cases, Black children had been denied admission to schools attended by white children, under laws “requiring or permitting segregation according to race.” The cases came from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia and Delaware.”* Ask who was allowed to go to which school: a true story that ends with the Court changing the law.
steps.purpose: Set out what the Brown cases were about.
students: Who was allowed to go to which school?
Where did the cases come from?

steps.title: The doll tests
script: Walk through the doll tests on the screen, row by row. A psychologist studies how people think and feel. Ask: *“Why do you think the dolls were the same in every way except their color?”* (Color is the only difference: a fair test.) After the crayons, give a moment of quiet, then ask where a child of three might have learned that. The Clarks named it: *prejudice, discrimination and segregation.*

screen.caption: Kenneth and Mamie Phipps Clark’s doll tests

cells: Kenneth and Mamie Phipps Clark, psychologists, in the 1940s
Four plastic dolls, identical except for color, shown to Black children aged three to seven
Which dolls were “nice” and which were “bad,” and which doll was most like them
National Park Service · Library of Congress
Almost all knew the race of the dolls; a majority preferred the white doll
Many children with dark complexions colored a drawing of themselves white or yellow
“Prejudice, discrimination, and segregation” created a feeling of inferiority and damaged self-esteem

steps.purpose: Read what the Clarks did, and found, from the room’s checked facts.
students: Why do you think the dolls were the same in every way except their color?
Where might young children have learned which doll was “nice”?

steps.title: Into court
script: Then the study went to court: Thurgood Marshall asked the Clarks to repeat their experiments in Clarendon County, and Kenneth Clark became the NAACP Legal Defense Fund’s principal expert witness. Ask: *“Why would lawyers ask a psychologist, and not only teachers and parents, to speak in court?”*

screen.question: Why would lawyers ask a psychologist, and not only teachers and parents, to speak in court?

steps.purpose: See how a study became evidence in a case.
students: Why might a court need one?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three follow the doll tests from the study to the Court.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Put six events in order, match six key words to their meanings, explain why the dolls were identical except for color, and finish two sentences about the decision.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Read the Court’s own words as a primary source, complete a chain of evidence from the study to the decision, and explain why the doll test was only one part of Clark’s testimony.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh each part of the study for what it can and cannot show, explain why the Court cited Clark in a footnote, and argue why the exhibition sets the Doll Test beside the Black Barbie poster.

steps.purpose: Work with the evidence at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three follow the doll tests from the study to the Court.

steps.title: From study to decision
script: Groups name the link in the chain that matters most, and why. Read: *“Because of their impact on the Court’s decision, the doll tests have become a symbol of the Brown case.”* Ask a Red Level reader why.

steps.purpose: Pull the chain of evidence together, and weigh it.
students: Which link in the chain matters most? Why?
Why have the doll tests become a symbol of the case?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
